claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel possesses a native surface oxide layer.
The Q235 samples initially have an unmodified microstructure.
At room temperature and approximately 700 °C, Q235 corrosion resistance derives from the maintained integrity of a thin native oxide film.
Dense surface oxide films can act as protective corrosion barriers.
Na2SO4/NaCl exposure at 800–900 °C causes salt-assisted fluxing and thermally activated degradation of the Q235 oxide.
Salt-driven fluxing causes selective leaching and phase transformations within the Q235 oxide film.
Selective leaching and phase transformations cause oxide thinning, spallation, or compositional change.
Breakdown of the oxide barrier accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
Molten-salt corrosion can involve near-surface elemental dissolution and morphological changes that can be compared with a stainless-steel reference.
The proposed study exposes Q235 to 75% Na2SO4 plus 25% NaCl at room temperature, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.
In situ XRD and cross-sectional SEM/EDS will track oxide phase composition, morphology, thickness, and spallation.
At room temperature and near 700 °C, salt-exposed Q235 will exhibit minimal corrosion and stable oxide scales.
At 800–900 °C, salt-exposed Q235 will show increased mass loss, oxide breakdown or spallation, and non-protective corrosion products relative to no-salt Q235 or stainless-steel references.
The proposed degradation mechanism requires the combination of high temperature and an aggressive salt environment.
In an inert atmosphere or without salt, the native Q235 oxide should remain stable and protective even under the stated thermal regimes.
Stainless steel is an appropriate corrosion-resistant reference material.
Minor alloying elements and microstructural heterogeneities may influence the protective behavior of Q235.
The composition of the native Q235 oxide and its transformation pathways under combined thermal and salt stress are not fully established.
